1.a: Before I recommend anything, I want to understand your family rather than your balance sheet. I am going to ask you some questions I do not normally ask, and there are no wrong answers. What I write down stays between us until you tell me otherwise.
1.f: We are going to spend an hour answering some questions about our own family. Not about money. About who we are and where we came from. I want to hear your answers, not correct them.

2.a: Every family runs on a set of values whether they have named them or not. I want to help you name yours, because once they are on paper they can settle decisions that otherwise get argued every time.
2.f: I want us to name what we actually value as a family. Not what sounds good. What we would still choose on a hard day. Everyone gets to answer, and the youngest goes first.

3.a: You have spent decades building something. I want to ask what it was for, and what the next season is for. That question sits underneath every financial decision we will make together.
3.f: I have been thinking about what I am actually here to do with the years I have left. I want to say it out loud to you rather than keep it to myself.

4.a: Plans transfer through people, and the relationships carry the plan or they do not. I want to look honestly at where the relationships in this family are strong and where they are thin.
4.f: There is something between us I would rather name than keep working around. I am not looking to be right. I am looking to still be close to you in ten years.

5.a: I would like each of you to answer these separately before we talk. Most couples assume they agree about money and the future, and the assumption is where the trouble starts.
5.f: Let's each answer these on our own, then trade pages before we say anything. I want to know what you actually think, not what you think I want to hear.

6.a: Your children are learning about money and responsibility from what they watch, not from what you tell them. This gives you a way to be deliberate about what they are learning.
6.f: I want to be more intentional about what we are teaching you than I have been. Some of what you have picked up from me I chose, and some of it I did not.

7.a: This measures preparation, not worth. Every family I work with worries about this privately and almost none have said it out loud. Naming a specific gap is far kinder than a general worry.
7.f: I want to prepare you for what is coming rather than protect you from it. This is not a test and it is not a judgment. It is me taking your future seriously.

8.a: Most of what a family believes about money was inherited rather than chosen. I want to trace what you received, so we can decide together what is worth keeping.
8.f: I want to talk about how our family thinks about money. Some of it came from my parents and I have never really examined it. Let's look at it together.

9.a: The documents will do their work later. What only you can do is say your intentions out loud while you are still here to explain them. Let's plan that conversation before we draft anything further.
9.f: There will be decisions about what we have built, and someday they will be yours. I am not handing you numbers tonight. I want you to know what we hope it does, and what we hope it never does to this family.

10.a: Families do not fail over the decisions themselves. They fail over not knowing who decides. Let's write the rule now, while nobody is upset and it is only theoretical.
10.f: I want us to agree on how we make decisions together before we have to make a hard one. It is much easier to write this down now than in the middle of a disagreement.

11.a: Ownership and leadership are two different handoffs, and treating them as one is how families lose companies. I want to look at each of them separately with you.
11.f: We need to talk about the business as a family and not only as owners. I want to know what each of you actually wants, including the ones who do not want it.

12.a: This transition changes more than the finances. I want to plan the first year rather than the whole future, because that is the part people are least ready for.
12.f: Something is changing for us, and I would rather talk about it early than let it happen to us. Let's think about the next twelve months together.

13.a: Giving decided together forms a family in a way that writing a check alone never does. I want to help you make one giving decision as a family this year.
13.f: I want us to decide together where our family gives this year. Everyone gets a say, and the youngest person answers first.

14.a: Your convictions about ownership and stewardship should be shaping the plan rather than sitting alongside it. I want to hear them in your own words.
14.f: I want us to talk about what we believe God has entrusted to this family and what we think we are supposed to do with it. Not a lecture. A conversation.

15.a: How a family is actually doing matters as much as how the plan is doing. I want to look at the whole picture, and then choose one thing rather than all of it.
15.f: I want to check in on how we are really doing, not just how things look. Let's each be honest about one area that needs attention.

16.a: I have one question I want to ask you today, and then I mostly want to listen. You will not hurt my feelings by taking your time with it.
16.f: Our advisor asked me something this week that I have not been able to put down, and I want to ask you the same thing.

17.a: This meeting works when the agenda comes from the family's own answers rather than from me. Here is what I have drafted; tell me what to cut and what is missing.
17.f: We are going to sit down as a family for two hours. Here is the agenda ahead of time so nobody is surprised, and everyone will be asked to speak.

18.a: Every family is one generation from losing the stories that explain it. I would like to record this while your parents are able to tell it themselves.
18.f: I want to record you telling some of our family's story, while we can. Not to put it anywhere. Just so your grandchildren can hear it in your voice.

19.a: Let's look at what this year actually produced before we plan the next one, and let's put a name and a date on every line rather than an intention.
19.f: Let's look back at the year as a family and then choose two or three things for the next one. Whoever owns something gets to say so out loud.

20.a: This is built from what your family told us rather than from a template. Read it before anyone else does, and change whatever does not sound like you.
20.f: Someone put this together for our family specifically. It is a draft. If something in it is wrong about us, say so and we will change it.
